newsitem.title: USA: Jury begins deliberations in Army rape trial.
newsitem.headline: Jury begins deliberations in Army rape trial.

text.p: Jurors in the rape trial of Army Staff Sgt. Delmar Simpson began deliberations on Thursday in the highest-profile case of a sexual misconduct scandal at the Army's Aberdeen Proving Ground.

Deliberations by the six-member military jury followed closing arguments in which prosecution and defence lawyers battled over the credibility of alleged victims and the power of Army drill sergeants. Jurors later recessed until Friday morning.

Prosecutor Capt. Theresa Gallagher, seeking the Army's first rape conviction in the probe, described Simpson as a "mean, arrogant and manipulative" drill instructor who used "fear, intimidation and control" to rape six trainees at the proving ground's Ordnance Training Centre and School.

Defence lawyer Frank Spinner told jurors there was reason to doubt the testimony of all the alleged rape victims and said the military risked a breakdown in discipline if jurors convicted Simpson without stronger evidence.
"If you convict Staff Sgt. Simpson on facts like these you're going to be sending out a message into the Army that no drill sergeant is safe," he said.

"What this really comes down to is any woman can come in and say she had sex with a drill sergeant, and she was raped, without any corroborating evidence," he said. "Discipline is going to break down, if it hasn't already broken down, because who has the power now? The drill sergeant or the trainee?"

Simpson, 32, faces 19 counts of rape and 35 other counts of forcible sodomy, indecent assault and other offences. He is the first of 12 trainers charged in the Aberdeen probe to go to trial -- and the one facing the most rape charges.
He has pleaded innocent to rape and all other charges, but earlier pleaded guilty to 11 counts of improper sexual intercourse with trainees and five of propositioning.
He faces a maximum of life in prison if convicted of rape and a total of 32 years, dishonourable discharge and forfeiture of pay and allowances for the counts to which he has pleaded guilty.
A guilty verdict on any charge requires a 4-2 jury majority.
Simpson's lawyers have argued any sexual relationships were consensual.
But Gallagher, in an 80-minute closing statement, described in explicit, sometimes earthy, detail the prosecution's version of how Simpson allegedly raped each woman, and some repeatedly.

"This is a case of rape. This is a case of the accused using his power, his easy access and his ability to control -- an unscrupulous drill sergeant grossly misusing his position to force his sexual attentions on trainees," she said.

Citing testimony of the women, she drew a picture of harshly forced sex in Simpson's office or elsewhere with limbs restrained by the accused, crying hushed by his commands and physical injury to the victims.
She said Simpson became increasingly aggressive and forceful in pursuing sex with trainees.
"He becomes more perverted, more aggressive, more demanding over time as he becomes more experienced and more comfortable in his role as a drill sergeant," she said.

But Spinner methodically challenged the testimony of each woman, calling attention to inconsistencies and saying they all had motives to turn what was consensual sex into stories of force and pressure when told to the court or investigators.

"There is no physical, objective evidence that rape occurred," he said. He said the women may have lied about rape for several reasons such as concealing a consensual relationship from others or retaliating for bad treatment.

Spinner also accused the prosecution of being paternalistic. "What the government seems to be saying is that women are too weak or too ignorant to know what to do when a man tells them he wants to have sex with them," he said.
